title: Interpretability Folklore: Attention Maps, Probes and Features on Trial
dek: Attention heatmaps, linear probes and sparse features are the three tools everyone reaches for. Each one answers a narrower question than the folklore says.
by: Draft for team review · written by Claude Code from published research and engineering writing · checked in code
lead: What is mechanistic interpretability? Finding the internal parts that cause a behavior, then testing them by intervention. Attention maps, probes and sparse features are leads; ablations and targeted edits are the evidence.

cover.alt: A glowing heatmap sheet peeled back at one corner to reveal a wiring diagram of nodes beneath, with one lit path.
cover.caption: The heatmap is the surface people read; the mechanism is the wiring underneath it.

description: What is mechanistic interpretability, and which beliefs survive? Attention maps, probes, sparse features and circuit tuning, checked against new papers.
decisions: Treat an attention map as a lead, then confirm it with an ablation.
Report probe results as readability, never as use.
Select sparse features on some prompt variants and test on others.
Restrict fine-tuning to components you have causally located.
Test a suspected shortcut internally when outputs look clean.

items.myth: The attention map shows what the model is thinking.
items.reality: Under negation, models do not follow human-like attention, and one attention shift that looked like the mechanism was a byproduct under headwise ablation.

items.myth: If a linear probe can read it, the model uses it.
items.reality: A probe shows a property is readable; a change in representation need not affect a downstream computation, so use needs an intervention.

items.myth: A sparse autoencoder feature keeps its meaning across rephrasings.
items.reality: Prompt rewrites that keep the request can redistribute activity across features, and one observed change need not recur.

items.myth: Interpretability explains models but cannot improve them.
items.reality: TITAN tunes fewer than 5% of parameters inside causally important circuits and reports large BLEU gains on low-resource translation.

items.myth: Multilingual models translate by thinking in English first.
items.reality: For Hindi to Urdu and Sindhi, translation runs through circuits over a shared semantic subspace, with no English-centric pivot.

items.myth: A skill lives in a few components you can find.
items.reality: Single heads, small head subsets and sparse circuits keep turning up, but held-out and cross-architecture tests are still thin.

acknowledgement: Thank you to arXiv for use of its open access interoperability.

body.text: Attention shows where a model looks, not how it decides

body: Ask how to see inside a vision-language model and you'll hear it fast: just look at the attention map. It shows what the model looks at, so it shows what the model thinks. The crack appears with one word. Tell the model there is no dog in the picture. Where should it look now?

body.alt: Affirmative and negated panels; attention moves to the other object, and ablating those heads leaves negation intact.
body.caption: Attention can shift under negation without that shift doing the work, which is what headwise ablation tests.

body: our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism

Attention is the weight each head, one of many parallel attention units in a layer, puts on every input position. A new arXiv paper on negation compared those weights with human eye fixations. The authors find «models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention». The map and the reasoning came apart.

The best moment is a near miss. PaliGemma2-3B does move object attention to the alternative under negation. It looks exactly like the mechanism. Then come ablations, which switch off chosen heads and watch what breaks. The verdict: «our headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism». Plausible map, no causal role.

To be fair, attention sometimes does point at the culprit. A new arXiv paper on chest X-rays found one head «attending to corner text rather than lung pathology in 62% of 200 COVID-19 images». What made that credible was the follow-up: inpainting the text away and measuring the change. We think that's the rule. An attention map is a lead to chase, never a verdict.

body.text: A probe proves a signal is readable, and stops there

body: Next belief: if a linear probe can read a property from activations, the model must be using it. A linear probe is a single linear layer trained on frozen hidden states to predict a label. It's cheap and it's everywhere. It also answers a narrower question than people assume.

A new arXiv paper on damping shows the narrow question well. It probes frozen encoders for the quality factor Q, «a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations an object completes before its ring dies away». The score is Spearman's ρ, a rank correlation where 1 means perfect ordering. Audio embeddings reach 0.73. One CLIP-encoded video frame manages 0.28. So the property is readable from sound, much less from a frame.

We like what the authors did next. Having «established where the signal lives», they asked a causal question: can vision be taught it? Distilling a frozen audio teacher into frozen CLIP, with whole materials held out, «improves the correlation there from 0.234 to 0.338». Widening to four frames «supplies half of that improvement at no acoustic cost». The probe located the signal. Training tested it.

The general warning comes from a paper on sparse features. Its authors write that «even a recurring change need not affect a downstream computation». Readable is a fact about the representation. Used is a fact about behavior. Only an intervention connects them: an ablation, a patch, a targeted edit.

body.label: Readable versus used, as illustrative pseudo-code
body.source:
# Illustrative pattern, not a library API
# Question A: is the property readable here?
probe = fit_linear(hidden_train[layer], labels_train)
readable = probe.score(hidden_test[layer], labels_test)

# Question B: does the model use this component?
baseline = task_metric(model, eval_inputs)
ablated = task_metric(model.without(component), eval_inputs)
used = baseline - ablated      # no change means not causally needed here

# A high 'readable' with a zero 'used' is the common, confusing case.

body.caption: How well frozen embeddings order impacts by damping, as Spearman rank correlation with Q.

body.text: A feature label can slip under a harmless paraphrase

body: A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is a second network trained to rewrite a layer's activations as a few active features out of many. Each feature, ideally, means one thing. The belief goes like this: label a feature once and the label holds. Reword the prompt, keep the request, and the same features fire.

body.alt: Two rows of feature cells for an original and a reworded prompt, with active cells moving to different positions.
body.caption: A paraphrase that keeps the request can move activity to different features, so a label from one prompt may not transfer.

body: A new arXiv paper on representation redistribution says that's shaky. Prompt rewrites «designed to preserve the underlying request can redistribute activity across them», shifting weight from one set of features to another. Worse, «A feature change observed on one transformed prompt need not recur». One example tells you little.

We went through how the authors separate signal from noise. Their redistribution sensitivity score (RSS) «identifies large feature responses that recur in a consistent direction». They choose supports on some prompt variants, then score them on variants excluded from selection. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, the redistribution profile held on those excluded variants. That held-out step is the part worth stealing.

Does the shift matter downstream? Two frozen safety readouts, linear classifiers on top of the features, make the test. AUROC measures how well a score ranks failures above successes. RSS support erosion reaches 0.935 and 0.958 with median supports of 20 and 19 features. Full erosion reaches 0.965 and 0.964. In our view the restraint is the headline: they measure impact «without equating representation change with failure».

body.caption: Recurrent failure AUROC on two frozen safety readouts, from a few RSS-selected features against full erosion.

body.text: Circuits can be tuned as well as read

body: Here's a belief skeptics repeat: interpretability is a microscope, nice for papers and useless for shipping. A circuit, for this post, is the small set of components that carries one behavior. If you can find it, can you train only it? Two new arXiv papers say yes.

body.alt: A grid of transformer components, mostly locked, with a small located circuit highlighted and trained.
body.caption: Circuit-restricted tuning updates only the located components and leaves the rest of the network frozen.

body: TITAN targets low-resource translation, Hindi to Urdu and Hindi to Sindhi. It combines «causal intervention, sparse feature decomposition, and targeted preference optimization». Then it «restricts optimization to sparse, causally important circuits», updating fewer than 5% of model parameters. BLEU, an overlap score against reference translations, improves by 33.75% and 45.86% over the strongest multilingual baselines.

The second paper works with heads. It ranks attention heads «by gradient norm to identify a small subset of heads that can be trained effectively». Tuning higher-ranked heads «consistently outperforms tuning lower-ranked ones while often matching denser baselines». Splitting heads between tasks also helps old skills survive.

We agree with the direction, with one caveat. Gradient norm is a training signal, not a causal test. It says where learning is cheap, not what a head means. Still, the microscope myth doesn't survive these results.

body.text: Translation in these models skips the English detour

body: A popular belief about multilingual models: they quietly route everything through English. It's intuitive, since English dominates training text. For the Hindi pairs TITAN studied, the analysis disagrees. Translation «is implemented through sparse, structured circuits operating over a shared semantic subspace rather than through an English-centric pivot representation».

A shared semantic subspace is a region of activation space where meaning sits regardless of language. Our caveat is about distance. Hindi, Urdu and Sindhi are close relatives, so a shared space is the easy case. A distant pair could tell another story. That test isn't in the abstract, so we'd call the myth busted only for these pairs.

body.text: Some skills may really live in a handful of parts

body: Here's the belief we suspect will survive: a given skill lives in a few components, and you can find them. The evidence leans that way. TITAN's circuits touch under 5% of parameters. Head ranking finds small trainable subsets. The X-ray work found a single head, L8H10, that «functions as a dedicated annotation-reader on chest X-rays».

That last case also shows why outputs alone can't settle the question. Ablating one head gave p = 0.340 on output metrics, and ablating all three carriers gave 0.532. The authors conclude the circuit is «completely invisible to output-level evaluation». A behavioral test said nothing was there. The mechanism said otherwise.

What would settle it? Three kinds of evidence. A circuit found on some prompts should predict behavior on held-out prompts, the way RSS scores excluded variants. Editing only the circuit should move the skill, as TITAN does. And the finding should replicate across architectures, as that head did on ViT-Base 16, DeiT-Base and ViT-Large 16. Get all three and the belief graduates.

Mechanistic interpretability finds the internal components that cause a model's behavior and tests them by intervention. Researchers locate candidate heads, features or circuits, then ablate, patch or retrain them to see what changes. One chest X-ray study argued that «Mechanistic auditing finds what behavioural testing cannot», because a located shortcut never showed up in output metrics.
Do attention maps explain how a model makes decisions?

Not on their own; they show where weight goes, not what causes the answer. A study of negation found models «rely on mechanisms outside of attention», and an attention shift that looked meaningful was a byproduct under ablation. Use attention to find candidates, then switch components off and measure what breaks.
Are sparse autoencoder features reliable for interpretability?

They are useful, but a feature's activity can move when you merely rephrase the prompt. Rewrites that keep the request can redistribute activity across features. The redistribution sensitivity score keeps only changes that recur in a consistent direction, and tests them on prompt variants excluded from selection before trusting them.
